slides.title: Mathematics — Quadratic Vertex-Form Transformations
slides.purpose: Explore how a, h, and k transform y = a(x - h)^2 + k compared to the reference curve y = x^2.
onScreenText: y = a(x - h)² + k vs reference y = x²
h shifts horizontally; k shifts vertically
a controls width and opening direction

visual.altText: Quadratic vertex form equation y = a(x - h)^2 + k with vertex at (h, k)
visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="400" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="42" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">y = a(x - h)² + k</text><text x="400" y="265" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#0284c7">Vertex at (h, k) · Compare directly against y = x²</text></svg>

narration.script: Adjust a, h, and k in the Graph and Slider Lab below to compare the transformed parabola against the dashed reference parabola y equals x squared.

keyIdeas: Changing h shifts the vertex horizontally; k shifts vertically; a stretches or reflects.

interactive.title: Discover Quadratic Vertex Form
interactive.instructions: Move a, h, and k to see how the vertex (h, k) and curvature compare with the reference parabola y = x².
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Quadratic vertex form graph and parameter sliders
interactive.fallbackText: In y = a(x - h)^2 + k, the vertex sits at (h, k). Negative a flips the parabola upside down; |a| > 1 narrows it.
interactive.modelNote: Real-valued quadratic function plotted over x in [-6, 6].

challenges.prompt: Make the parabola open downward (a < 0) with its vertex at (2, 4).
challenges.successText: Well done! Because a < 0, the vertex (2, 4) is a maximum point.
challenges.hintText: Set a to a negative value, h = 2, and k = 4.

slides.title: Physics — Projectile Motion Trajectory & Range
slides.purpose: Investigate how launch angle and initial speed control horizontal range and maximum height.
onScreenText: Idealised trajectory with landing bisection
Complementary angles (30° & 60°) share equal range
45° maximises horizontal range on level ground

visual.altText: Projectile launch schematic showing angle theta and initial speed v0
visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f0f9ff"/><text x="400" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="36" font-weight="bold" fill="#0c4a6e">Projectile Motion Lab</text><text x="400" y="255" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#0369a1">R = v₀² sin(2θ) / g · H = v₀² sin²(θ) / (2g)</text></svg>

narration.script: Experiment with launch angle and initial speed. Compare 30 degrees, 45 degrees, and 60 degrees while keeping initial speed fixed at 26 metres per second.

keyIdeas: Horizontal range is maximised at 45°; 30° and 60° give identical horizontal range.

interactive.title: Discover Projectile Motion
interactive.instructions: Adjust launch angle and initial speed to observe how the trajectory, range, and maximum height respond.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Projectile motion trajectory graph and sliders
interactive.fallbackText: With constant g = 9.81 m/s² and no air resistance on level ground, horizontal range is maximised at 45° and complementary angles (30° and 60°) yield equal range.
interactive.modelNote: Idealised projectile motion: g = 9.81 m/s², no air resistance, equal launch and landing heights.

challenges.prompt: Keep initial speed at 26 m/s and set the launch angle that gives the greatest horizontal range.
challenges.successText: Exact! At θ = 45° and v₀ = 26 m/s, sin(2θ) = 1, giving the maximum range of 68.91 m.
challenges.hintText: Make sure initial speed stays at 26 m/s and compare 30°, 45°, and 60°.

slides.title: Physics — Discover Ohm's Law (Predict → Experiment)
slides.purpose: Demonstrate Predict -> Experiment -> Observe -> Compare -> Explain flow with reference resistance curve.
onScreenText: I = V / R for an ideal ohmic resistor
Predict before testing resistance doubling
Compare against dashed 3 Ω reference line

visual.altText: Ohm's Law relationship I = V / R
visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#fefce8"/><text x="400" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="44" font-weight="bold" fill="#713f12">I = V / R</text><text x="400" y="262" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#a16207">Predict, then test how resistance affects current</text></svg>

narration.script: First predict what happens to current when resistance doubles at constant voltage, then test your prediction with the Voltage and Resistance sliders.

keyIdeas: At constant voltage, doubling resistance halves the current.

interactive.title: How Does Resistance Affect Current?
interactive.instructions: Compare the current-voltage graph for your chosen resistance R against the dashed 3 Ω reference resistor.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Ohm's Law current versus voltage graph and sliders
interactive.fallbackText: By Ohm's Law (I = V / R), keeping voltage at 6 V and doubling resistance from 3 Ω to 6 Ω halves the current from 2.00 A to 1.00 A.
interactive.modelNote: Ideal ohmic resistor with constant resistance at each setting.

prediction.prompt: A circuit has V = 6 V and R = 3 Ω (current = 2 A). What happens to current if resistance doubles to 6 Ω at constant 6 V?
prediction.explanation: Current is inversely proportional to resistance (I = V / R), so doubling R halves I.

challenges.prompt: Set Test Voltage to 6 V and Resistance to 6 Ω to confirm the current drops to 1.00 A.
challenges.successText: Confirmed! At 6 V and 6 Ω, I = 6 / 6 = 1.00 A — half the original 2.00 A.
challenges.hintText: Set Test Voltage = 6 V and Resistance = 6 Ω.

slides.title: NaCCA Science — Transverse Wave Properties
slides.purpose: Explore spatial wave snapshot y(x) = A sin(2πx / λ) and wave speed v = fλ.
onScreenText: Spatial snapshot: y(x) = A sin(2πx / λ)
Amplitude A changes height, not wavelength λ
Wave speed v = fλ and Period T = 1/f

visual.altText: Transverse wave equation y(x) = A sin(2 pi x / lambda)
visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#ecfeff"/><text x="400" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="36" font-weight="bold" fill="#155e75">y(x) = A sin(2πx / λ)</text><text x="400" y="258" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#0e7490">Spatial snapshot at fixed time · v = fλ · T = 1/f</text></svg>

narration.script: Explore this spatial snapshot of a transverse wave. Notice how amplitude changes crest height while wavelength changes the distance between consecutive crests.

keyIdeas: Amplitude and wavelength are independent properties of a spatial wave snapshot.

interactive.title: Discover the Properties of a Transverse Wave
interactive.instructions: Vary Amplitude (A), Wavelength (λ), and Frequency (f) to observe the spatial wave snapshot and calculated wave speed.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Transverse wave spatial snapshot graph and sliders
interactive.fallbackText: In a spatial wave snapshot y(x) = A sin(2πx / λ), amplitude A sets peak height, wavelength λ sets crest-to-crest distance, wave speed is v = fλ, and period is T = 1/f.
interactive.modelNote: Spatial snapshot at a fixed instant in time (not a time graph). Frequency changes the calculated wave speed v = fλ and period T = 1/f rather than the frozen spatial shape.

challenges.prompt: Double the amplitude to 2 m while keeping wavelength at 2 m. Notice the crests stay 2 m apart.
challenges.successText: Exactly! Increasing amplitude makes the wave taller without changing its wavelength.
challenges.hintText: Set Amplitude = 2 m and keep Wavelength = 2 m.

slides.title: Economics — Supply & Demand Market Equilibrium
slides.purpose: Demonstrate Economics applicability with two intersecting curves and live equilibrium price/quantity readouts.
onScreenText: Demand: P = d₀ - Q · Supply: P = s₀ + Q
Equilibrium where Supply meets Demand
Shift demand upward to observe price & quantity rise

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f0fdf4"/><text x="400" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="36" font-weight="bold" fill="#14532d">Supply & Demand Equilibrium</text><text x="400" y="258" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#166534">P_d = d₀ - Q · P_s = s₀ + Q</text></svg>

narration.script: Shift the demand and supply intercepts to observe how market equilibrium price and quantity respond.

keyIdeas: Higher demand with unchanged supply raises both equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity.

interactive.title: Explore Market Equilibrium
interactive.instructions: Adjust the demand and supply intercepts to watch the intersection point and equilibrium readouts shift.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Supply and demand market equilibrium graph
interactive.fallbackText: For linear curves P_d = d₀ - Q and P_s = s₀ + Q, equilibrium occurs at Q* = (d₀ - s₀)/2 and P* = (d₀ + s₀)/2.
interactive.modelNote: Simplified linear market model with all other market conditions held constant (ceteris paribus).

challenges.prompt: Hold Supply intercept at 20 GH₵ and raise Demand intercept to 100 GH₵. Confirm equilibrium price reaches 60 GH₵.
challenges.successText: Correct! With stronger demand (d₀ = 100) and unchanged supply (s₀ = 20), P* rises from 50 to 60 GH₵ and Q* rises from 30 to 40 units.
challenges.hintText: Keep Supply = 20 GH₵ and move Demand to 100 GH₵.

slides.title: NaCCA Science — Piecewise Distance–Time Graph
slides.purpose: Demonstrate bounded declarative piecewise plotting (walk -> stationary rest -> walk faster).
onScreenText: 0–4 s: steady walk (10 m/s)
4–7 s: stationary rest (0 m/s, flat line)
7–10 s: faster walk (20 m/s, steeper slope)

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="400" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="34" font-weight="bold" fill="#0f172a">Piecewise Distance–Time Graph</text><text x="400" y="258" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#475569">Gradient = Speed · Horizontal line = Stationary</text></svg>

narration.script: Inspect the three stages of this pupil's walk using the coordinate inspector and data table. A horizontal segment means the pupil is stationary.

keyIdeas: Steeper gradient on a distance-time graph represents greater speed; flat segment means zero speed.

interactive.title: Piecewise Distance–Time Journey
interactive.instructions: Scrub the coordinate inspector across 0 to 10 seconds and open the data table to compare speeds in each stage.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Piecewise distance-time graph of a three-stage journey
interactive.fallbackText: Stage 1 (0–4 s): 40 m at 10 m/s. Stage 2 (4–7 s): stationary at 40 m (0 m/s). Stage 3 (7–10 s): 60 m in 3 s (20 m/s).
interactive.modelNote: Declarative piecewise linear segments (no executable conditions).

slides.title: Mathematics — Discontinuities: Reciprocal & Tangent
slides.purpose: Verify clean asymptote segmentation for y = k/x and y = tan(x) with zero false connecting lines.
onScreenText: Reciprocal y = k / x has vertical asymptote at x = 0
Tangent y = tan(x) has asymptotes at x = ±π/2
Separate branches — zero false vertical connectors

visual.altText: Reciprocal and tangent asymptote verification header
visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#fdf2f8"/><text x="400" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="36" font-weight="bold" fill="#831843">y = k / x  and  y = tan(x)</text><text x="400" y="258" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#9d174d">Discontinuity segmentation across vertical asymptotes</text></svg>

narration.script: Observe how both the reciprocal curve and tangent curve separate cleanly across their vertical asymptotes without drawing false connecting lines.

keyIdeas: Vertical asymptotes split curves into separate branches.

interactive.title: Asymptote & Discontinuity Explorer
interactive.instructions: Adjust k to scale y = k / x and inspect how both y = k / x and y = tan(x) break cleanly across asymptotes.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Reciprocal and tangent function discontinuity graph
interactive.fallbackText: y = k / x is undefined at x = 0; y = tan(x) is undefined at odd multiples of π/2 (~ ±1.57). Branches do not connect across asymptotes.
interactive.modelNote: Angles for tan(x) are in radians; SVG clipPath prevents false horizontal clamping.

slides.title: Computer Science — Digital Signal Step Waveform
slides.purpose: Demonstrate step-line plotting (kind='step') for binary 0/1 digital signals without diagonal interpolation.
onScreenText: Binary sequence: 0 1 1 0 1 0
Step-line plotting holds level across equal bits
Vertical transitions between 0 (LOW) and 1 (HIGH)

visual.svgCode: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 450" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="800" height="450" fill="#0f172a"/><text x="400" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-family="monospace" font-size="36" font-weight="bold" fill="#38bdf8">Digital Signal: 0 1 1 0 1 0</text><text x="400" y="258" text-anchor="middle" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#94a3b8">Step-line plotting — discrete binary states</text></svg>

narration.script: Inspect this digital logic signal plotted with step-line transitions. Consecutive ones stay flat at HIGH without diagonal sloping.

keyIdeas: Digital signals transition discretely between LOW (0) and HIGH (1).

interactive.title: Digital Signal Step-Line Waveform
interactive.instructions: Use the time inspector to read the discrete binary state (0 = LOW, 1 = HIGH) at each clock interval.
interactive.accessibilityLabel: Digital signal binary step waveform graph
interactive.fallbackText: Binary sequence 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0 switches cleanly between 0 (LOW) and 1 (HIGH) at clock edges.
interactive.modelNote: Declarative step-line series (kind='step') — zero diagonal interpolation.

summary.recapScript: You have tested all 8 cross-subject Step 4A Graph and Slider pilots through a single reusable lazy-loaded engine.
